vjimc-2010-cat1-01.title: AM–GM for (a), an explicit involution for (b)
vjimc-2010-cat1-01.body:
**(a) Yes.** For every $n$, by AM–GM,
$$\frac1{n\,f(n)}\le\frac12\left(\frac1{n^2}+\frac1{f(n)^2}\right).$$
For each $N$ the numbers $f(1),\dots,f(N)$ are distinct positive integers, so $\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1{f(n)^2}\le\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac1{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}6$. Hence
$$\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{1}{n f(n)}\le\frac12\left(\frac{\pi^2}6+\frac{\pi^2}6\right)=\frac{\pi^2}6$$
for all $N$; the partial sums of this positive series are bounded, so it converges.

**(b)** Let $X=\mathbb N\setminus\{2,4,8,16,\dots\}=\{x_1<x_2<x_3<\dots\}=\{1,3,5,6,7,9,\dots\}$, an infinite set. Define
$$f(x_j)=2^j,\qquad f(2^j)=x_j\qquad(j\ge1).$$
Every positive integer is either some $x_j$ or some $2^j$ (and not both), and $f$ swaps $x_j$ with $2^j$; so $f$ is an involution of $\mathbb N$, in particular a bijection. Grouping the terms of the positive series in pairs $\{x_j,2^j\}$ (allowed for series of positive terms),
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n+f(n)}=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\left(\frac1{x_j+2^j}+\frac1{2^j+x_j}\right)=\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{2}{x_j+2^j}<\sum_{j=1}^\infty\frac{2}{2^j}=2 .$$
So the series converges. ∎

vjimc-2010-cat1-01.title: Rearrangement inequality for (a), greedy pairing for (b)
vjimc-2010-cat1-01.body:
**(a)** Fix $N$ and let $b_1<b_2<\dots<b_N$ be the values $f(1),\dots,f(N)$ in increasing order; then $b_j\ge j$. The sequences $\frac11\ge\frac12\ge\dots\ge\frac1N$ and $\frac1{b_1}\ge\dots\ge\frac1{b_N}$ are similarly ordered, so by the rearrangement inequality
$$\sum_{n=1}^N\frac1n\cdot\frac1{f(n)}\le\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1j\cdot\frac1{b_j}\le\sum_{j=1}^N\frac1{j^2}<\frac{\pi^2}6 .$$
The partial sums are bounded, so the series converges.

**(b)** Build pairs greedily: at step $j=1,2,\dots$ let $p_j$ be the smallest number not used yet and $q_j$ the smallest unused number greater than $\max(p_j,2^j)$; mark both as used and set $f(p_j)=q_j$, $f(q_j)=p_j$. At step $j$ the smallest unused number is taken, so by induction all of $1,\dots,j$ are used after step $j$; hence every positive integer is in exactly one pair and $f$ is a bijection (an involution). Then
$$\sum_n\frac1{n+f(n)}=\sum_j\frac{2}{p_j+q_j}<\sum_j\frac{2}{2^j}=2. \qquad ∎$$

vjimc-2010-cat1-02.title: Traces and Cayley–Hamilton
vjimc-2010-cat1-02.body:
For a $2\times2$ matrix, Cayley–Hamilton gives $B^2=(\operatorname{tr}B)\,B-(\det B)\,I$. Also
$$\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\operatorname{tr}(AB)-\operatorname{tr}(BA)=0 .$$

**$B$ is not invertible.** Otherwise $AB=BA+B^2=B(A+B)$ gives $A=B(A+B)B^{-1}$, so $\operatorname{tr}A=\operatorname{tr}(A+B)=\operatorname{tr}A+\operatorname{tr}B$ and $\operatorname{tr}B=0$. Then $B^2=-(\det B)I$ and $0=\operatorname{tr}B^2=-2\det B$, so $\det B=0$ — a contradiction.

So $\det B=0$ and $B^2=(\operatorname{tr}B)B$. Taking traces, $0=\operatorname{tr}B^2=(\operatorname{tr}B)^2$, so $\operatorname{tr}B=0$ and $B^2=0$. Hence $AB-BA=B^2=0$. ∎

vjimc-2010-cat1-02.title: Eigenvalues via traces of powers
vjimc-2010-cat1-02.body:
For $k\ge1$,
$$\operatorname{tr}\big(B^{k+1}\big)=\operatorname{tr}\big((AB-BA)B^{k-1}\big)=\operatorname{tr}(AB^k)-\operatorname{tr}(B\,AB^{k-1})=0,$$
since $\operatorname{tr}(B\cdot AB^{k-1})=\operatorname{tr}(AB^{k-1}\cdot B)$. Let $\lambda,\mu$ be the eigenvalues of $B$. Then $\lambda^2+\mu^2=0$ and $\lambda^3+\mu^3=0$. Write $s=\lambda+\mu$, $p=\lambda\mu$: then $s^2-2p=0$ and $\lambda^3+\mu^3=s(s^2-3p)=-sp=0$. If $s=0$ then $p=s^2/2=0$; if $p=0$ then $s^2=0$. In both cases $s=p=0$, so $\lambda=\mu=0$.

Thus the characteristic polynomial of $B$ is $x^2$, and by Cayley–Hamilton $B^2=0$. Hence $AB-BA=0$. ∎

vjimc-2010-cat1-03.title: Integration by parts with a split near $x=1$
vjimc-2010-cat1-03.body:
Let $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$. Then $f'(x)=-\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\le0$ and $f''(x)=-(1-x^2)^{-3/2}<0$ on $[0,1)$, $f'(0)=0$, and $\int_0^1|f'|=f(0)-f(1)=1$ (an absolutely convergent improper integral). All integrations by parts below on $[0,1]$ are justified by working on $[0,b]$ and letting $b\to1^-$.

**Lemma.** Let $k>1$ and $g=\sin$ or $g=\cos$. Then $\left|\int_0^1f'(x)g(kx)\,dx\right|<\frac{3}{\sqrt k}$.

*Proof.* Let $a=\sqrt{1-1/k}\in(0,1)$; then $|f'(a)|=\frac{a}{\sqrt{1-a^2}}=\sqrt{k-1}<\sqrt k$ and $f(a)=\frac1{\sqrt k}$. Let $G$ be the antiderivative $G(x)=\frac{\sin kx}{k}$ of $\cos kx$, resp. $G(x)=-\frac{\cos kx}{k}$ of $\sin kx$; in both cases $|G|\le\frac1k$, and $f'(0)G(0)=0$ because $f'(0)=0$. Then
$$\left|\int_0^af'g(kx)\,dx\right|=\left|\big[f'G\big]_0^a-\int_0^af''G\,dx\right|\le\frac{|f'(a)|}k+\frac1k\int_0^a|f''|=\frac{2|f'(a)|}{k}<\frac{2}{\sqrt k},$$
using $\int_0^a|f''|=f'(0)-f'(a)=|f'(a)|$. And
$$\left|\int_a^1f'g(kx)\,dx\right|\le\int_a^1|f'|=f(a)-f(1)=\frac1{\sqrt k}.$$
Adding gives the lemma. $\square$

**(a)** Integrating by parts, with $f(1)=0$ and $\sin0=0$,
$$\int_0^1f(x)\cos kx\,dx=\Big[f(x)\frac{\sin kx}k\Big]_0^1-\frac1k\int_0^1f'(x)\sin kx\,dx=-\frac1k\int_0^1f'(x)\sin kx\,dx ,$$
whose absolute value is $<\frac1k\cdot\frac3{\sqrt k}$ by the lemma. So $c_1=3$ works.

**(b)** Similarly, with $f(0)=1$, $f(1)=0$,
$$I(k):=\int_0^1f(x)\sin kx\,dx=\Big[-f(x)\frac{\cos kx}k\Big]_0^1+\frac1k\int_0^1f'(x)\cos kx\,dx=\frac1k+\frac1k\int_0^1f'(x)\cos kx\,dx ,$$
so $I(k)>\frac1k\left(1-\frac3{\sqrt k}\right)\ge\frac1{2k}$ for $k\ge36$.

For $1<k\le36$ integrate by parts with the antiderivative $\frac{1-\cos kx}{k}$, which vanishes at $0$ (and $f(1)=0$):
$$k\,I(k)=\int_0^1\frac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,\big(1-\cos kx\big)\,dx=:\Phi(k).$$
The integrand is nonnegative, continuous on $[0,1)$ and positive except at isolated points, so $\Phi(k)>0$; it is dominated by the integrable function $\frac{2x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}$, so $\Phi$ is continuous on $[1,36]$ by dominated convergence, and $m=\min_{[1,36]}\Phi>0$.

Hence $k\,I(k)\ge\min\left(m,\frac12\right)$ for every $k>1$, and $c_2=\frac12\min\left(m,\frac12\right)$ gives $|I(k)|=I(k)>\frac{c_2}k$. ∎

(Numerically, $k^{3/2}\left|\int_0^1 f\cos kx\right|$ stays below about $1.3$ and $k\int_0^1f\sin kx$ stays above about $0.3$ on $(1,1000]$.)

vjimc-2010-cat1-04.title: Multiply a weird number by a large prime
vjimc-2010-cat1-04.body:
**$70$ is weird.** Its divisors are $1,2,5,7,10,14,35,70$, so $\sigma(70)=144\ge140$. A representation with $r>1$ cannot use $70$ itself, so it would be a subset of $\{1,2,5,7,10,14,35\}$ (sum $74$) with sum $70$; its complement would have sum $4$, but no subset of these numbers sums to $4$ ($1+2=3$, and all others exceed $4$). (Such an $n$ can be found by looking for $n=2pq$ with $\sigma(n)=2n+4$ and no divisors $3,4$: $3(p+1)(q+1)=4pq+4\iff(p-3)(q-3)=8$, giving $p=5$, $q=7$.)

**Claim.** If $n$ is weird and $p$ is a prime with $p>\sigma(n)$, then $pn$ is weird.

Since $p>\sigma(n)\ge n$, $p\nmid n$, so the divisors of $pn$ are the $d$ and the $pd$ for $d\mid n$, all distinct, and $\sigma(pn)=(p+1)\sigma(n)\ge2pn$.

Suppose $pn=\sum_{d\in I}d+p\sum_{d\in J}d$ with $I,J$ sets of divisors of $n$ and $|I|+|J|\ge2$. Then
$$\sum_{d\in I}d=p\Big(n-\sum_{d\in J}d\Big).$$
The left side lies in $[0,\sigma(n)]\subset[0,p)$ and is divisible by $p$, so it is $0$: $I=\emptyset$. Then $\sum_{d\in J}d=n$ with $|J|\ge2$ distinct divisors of $n$, contradicting the weirdness of $n$. So $pn$ is weird.

There are infinitely many primes $p>\sigma(70)=144$, and the numbers $70p$ are distinct weird numbers. Hence there are infinitely many weird numbers. ∎
